name: Distillation into a Small Model
question: Can a small model learn to do what the big one does?
summary: Distillation uses a large teacher model’s outputs on your real inputs as training data for a small student. Filter the teacher’s answers with a judge or verifier, optionally include its reasoning, and fine-tune the student, often with LoRA. Then route most traffic to the student and keep the teacher as a fallback. It is the usual way to turn an expensive frontier-model workload into an affordable one.
useCases: A narrow, high-volume task that a frontier model already does well
Cost or latency limits that rule out a large model on every call
Data that must stay on your own infrastructure

steps.text: An automatic checker and a sample review drop wrong answers. The student copies whatever it is shown.

steps.title: Keep the reasoning
steps.text: Training on the teacher’s rationale as well as its answer helps a small model learn how, not just what.

steps.text: The student answers when it is confident; hard or unusual queries go to the teacher. Here 80% of traffic stayed on the student.

steps.title: Compare before shifting traffic
steps.text: On held-out queries the student scored 91% against the teacher’s 92%, at ₹0.08 a query against ₹0.90.

pros: Cuts cost per query by an order of magnitude
Uses answers you already have in logs
The teacher stays as a fallback
cons: The student is capped below the teacher on hard cases
Teacher mistakes are copied unless filtered
Provider terms may restrict training on outputs
Another model to evaluate and maintain
avoidWhen: Low-volume tasks where the teacher is cheap enough

practice.scenario: A travel platform’s itinerary assistant ran on a frontier model at ₹0.90 a query. The team collected 50,000 of its answers, kept those an automatic checker and a sample review passed, and tuned an 8B student on them. The student scored 91% against the teacher’s 92% on held-out queries at ₹0.08. Routing 80% of traffic to the student, and hard or low-confidence cases to the teacher, cut the bill by about 70%.

industries.use: Itinerary answers from a small model, hard trips routed to the large one
Intent classification and form filling by a distilled model on-premises
Product Q&A at high volume with a frontier fallback

practice.analogy: An experienced chef writes down how they cook each dish, the best recipes are kept, and a junior cook trains on them. The junior handles the everyday menu; the chef still takes the difficult orders.

numericDrill.question: A frontier model answers 3 million queries a month at ₹0.90 each. A distilled student costs ₹0.08 a query and takes 80% of traffic; the rest stays on the frontier model. What share of the monthly bill is saved, in percent? (Ignore training cost.)

interview.question: Why filter the teacher’s outputs before distilling?
interview.answer: The student learns whatever it is shown, including the teacher’s mistakes. Keeping only answers that pass an automatic checker, a judge or a sample review raises the student’s quality and stops it copying errors. Including the teacher’s rationales can also help a small student learn how, not just what.

interview.question: How would you deploy a distilled model safely?
interview.answer: Route traffic to it gradually, starting with the easy, common intents, and keep the teacher as a fallback for low-confidence or unusual queries. Compare the student with the teacher on held-out and live samples, and check the provider’s terms on training with its outputs.

mistakes.fix: Route gradually with the teacher as fallback

quiz.question: What is distillation in this context?
options: Training a smaller student on a larger teacher’s outputs
quiz.explanation: The student learns from the teacher.

quiz.question: 3M queries at ₹0.90; a student at ₹0.08 takes 80%. About what share of the bill is saved?
quiz.explanation: ₹7.32 lakh against ₹27 lakh: about 72.9% saved.

quiz.question: Why filter the teacher’s answers first?
options: The student copies the teacher’s mistakes otherwise
quiz.explanation: The student learns what it sees.

quiz.question: What did “Distilling step-by-step” show?
options: Training on the teacher’s rationales lets small models match larger ones with less data
Students must be larger than teachers
quiz.explanation: Rationales add signal.

quiz.question: Which belong in a safe rollout of a distilled model? Select all that apply.
options: A held-out comparison with the teacher
Routing with the teacher as fallback
quiz.explanation: Compare first, then route gradually with a fallback.

quiz.question: A student scores 73% where the teacher scores 92%. What happens if it takes all traffic?
quiz.explanation: Blended accuracy follows the traffic share.

quiz.question: What should you check before training on a provider model’s outputs?
quiz.explanation: Some terms restrict training competing models.

quiz.question: Which traffic should go to the student first?
quiz.explanation: Start where the student is strongest.

quiz.question: How is a distilled student usually trained when the teacher is an API model?
options: SFT on the teacher’s text outputs
quiz.explanation: Black-box teachers give text, not logits.

quiz.question: What limits a student’s quality? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Teacher quality and student capacity bound results.

quiz.question: A router sends a query to the teacher when…
options: The student’s confidence is below a threshold
quiz.explanation: Low confidence goes to the fallback.

quiz.question: What is a main benefit of a distilled model besides cost?
options: Lower latency and the option to run on-premises
Guaranteed higher accuracy than the teacher
quiz.explanation: Small models are faster and easier to host.

quiz.question: Logged answers were rated correct by support agents. How do you use the ratings?
options: Keep only answers rated correct for training
quiz.explanation: Ratings filter the dataset.

quiz.question: The student is at 91% and the teacher at 92% on held-out queries. What should you verify next?
options: Performance on hard and rare cases
quiz.explanation: Averages can hide failures on the tail.

quiz.question: Which TRL method distils using the teacher’s token probabilities?
quiz.explanation: GKD uses the teacher’s distributions.

quiz.question: Why might a hospital prefer a distilled model?
options: It can run inside its own network for data protection
quiz.explanation: On-premises hosting keeps data in-house.

quiz.question: More teacher answers help the student until…
options: It approaches the limit set by its size and the teacher
The GPU runs out of colours
quiz.explanation: Returns diminish.

quiz.question: The student is strong on 40 intents but weak on others. What is a sensible design?
options: Route those 40 intents to it and the rest to the teacher
quiz.explanation: Route by strength.

quiz.question: What is the teacher’s role after rollout?
options: Fallback for hard cases and source of new training data
quiz.explanation: The teacher stays useful.

quiz.question: Which is NOT a reason to distil?
options: The teacher is already cheap enough at your volume
quiz.explanation: If cost is fine, distillation adds work for little gain.
